title: Terrain Elevation Grid Map: Slopes Cell by Cell
description: Explore rough slope estimates from a grid of modelled elevations; not for engineering or access decisions.
summary_sentence: The slope display is a coarse estimate, not a guarantee of safe access, drainage or buildability.
quick_answer: The tool samples elevations on a 9×9 grid and colors the inner 7×7 cells by the largest elevation difference to a cardinal neighbor divided by spacing. This coarse estimate can miss steep or hazardous features.

body.t: A coarse slope grid can suggest where to investigate further. It does not assess vehicle or wheelchair access or foundations.
A grid can give a rough terrain overview, but it does not establish a route’s safety or difficulty. Check local conditions and reliable maps.
Slope samples alone do not determine drainage, flooding or soil conditions. Use qualified assessment and authoritative data.
Compare rough sampled gradients with contours as an educational exercise; sampling may miss features.
Changing the area size changes the distance between samples. A narrow steep feature can be missed even at the smallest available span.
A band of higher sample gradients may suggest terrain changes, but it does not identify a scarp, road cut or a particular landform.

faq: Detail follows the area you choose: the 9×9 grid divides your selected area, so small areas give metre-scale cells and large areas give broad-brush cells. The elevation source itself resolves features down to roughly 90 m in its underlying model.
Why the maximum gradient per cell?
Water, wheels and feet all care about the steepest direction, not the average. Each cell reports its steepest downhill gradient so hazards are not averaged away.
Can I get one exact slope instead?
A calculator can estimate grade from the inputs you provide, but precision and accuracy depend on how those elevations and distances were measured.
What elevation data does it use?
Open-Meteo's elevation sampling, built on global terrain models (Copernicus-class data). The atlas sibling samples a 7×7 grid of raw elevations from the same source family.
Does vegetation or buildings affect it?
Terrain models aim for bare earth, but processing varies; dense forest canopy and dense urban areas can bias sampled heights in the source data.
Water surfaces read at their surface elevation with near-zero slope — flat blue honesty at the grid's edge.
The grid is computed in your browser for viewing. For GIS work, the same public elevation sources can be loaded directly into QGIS or similar tools.
